unit: One camshaft position sensor, fitted. Many engines have two or more (one per bank, or one each for the intake and exhaust camshafts); this is the price for one. The Chrysler time used here is printed as "Inspect and Replace": it includes reading the serial number on the old sensor, and the bulletin's procedure ends with a cam/crank variation relearn on the scan tool. Not included: diagnosis of the warning light, long crank or stall, the crankshaft position sensor, wiring or connector repair, and the variable valve timing solenoid.

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. HELD: the economy and luxury classes have no labor time printed with a unit. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): midsize 2014 Jeep Cherokee 3.2L V6 about $75-$212 (0.4 hr); truck 2014 Ram 1500 3.6L V6 about $87-$228 (0.5 hr); economy and luxury not built. Against the benchmarks: Jerry ($127-$203) sits inside both built ranges; RepairPal ($224-$326) starts at about the top of ours. Two things explain the gap. RepairPal carries $107-$157 in labor, about 0.7-1.3 hours at this rate, against our 0.4-0.5 hour of warranty time, and a warranty time is the low end of what a shop bills; and our low end is a $26.99 budget-brand sensor, where RepairPal's parts start at $117. With the genuine sensor ($148.00 list) the two built vehicles come to about $196-$228. A supportable first range for one easy-to-reach sensor on a mainstream vehicle is roughly $75-$326, taking our low and RepairPal's high, and it should say plainly that it is for one sensor: many engines have two to four, and a shop may recommend the set. It should not be read as covering a buried sensor: Honda's own time for a camshaft position sensor on the 2005-09 Odyssey V6 is 4.5 hours because the timing belt comes off, and YourMechanic's Lexus ES350 rows ($468-$1,397) point the same way. How solid the labor times are: both come from one Chrysler bulletin (18-054-14) on NHTSA, are for the example vehicles, and are printed in hours against a sensor replacement op, so they are the maker's own numbers. Their limits: the op is "Inspect and Replace", so it includes reading the old sensor's serial number (the inspect-only op is 0.2 hour, which suggests the replacement itself is quick); it is for the bank 1 sensor only; the same bulletin gives 0.3 hour on six other models; and it lists no separate time for the relearn its procedure calls for. Each built class rests on that single time, so each range is narrow. Parts: the genuine Mopar sensor is $148.00 list for both vehicles; the low end is one aftermarket sensor stated as new whose page names the vehicles by year range but not the engine. What is missing and why: (1) economy hours: no bulletin replacing a camshaft position sensor on an economy car with a time in hours was found; the nearest figures are a Subaru Impreza and a Scion FR-S sensor shim job (0.5 and 0.6, printed with no unit, sensor refitted not replaced) and a 2003 Nissan Sentra campaign that fits a whole sensor kit in 0.5 hrs., all cross-checks only; (2) luxury hours: Audi's camshaft sensor campaign says "SEE ELSA" in place of a time, Jaguar Land Rover and GM (Cadillac) bulletins loaded cover the cam phaser or camshaft end play, not the sensor, and Hyundai prints times with no unit; (3) the luxury class has one parts source and the economy low end is a discounted genuine sensor, not an aftermarket one; (4) the midsize and truck examples are 2014 Chrysler-group vehicles sharing one engine family and one part number, so the two built classes are not independent. To finish: find a maker time with a unit for an economy car and a luxury car (Nissan/Infiniti, Honda/Acura and Ford/Lincoln bulletins print units), and load aftermarket prices from pages that state the part is new and name the engine. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee, because the same warning light, long crank or stall can come from wiring, the connector, a stretched timing chain, the variable valve timing solenoid or the crankshaft sensor. It may also add a cam/crank relearn with a scan tool, a new O-ring, shop supplies and sales tax. Engines with more than one camshaft sensor (one per bank, or separate intake and exhaust sensors) often get a recommendation to replace the set, which multiplies the parts cost and adds some labor. Where the sensor sits under an intake manifold, behind a timing cover or at the back of the engine against the firewall, removing and refitting those parts adds labor (Honda allows 4.5 hours on a 2005-09 Odyssey V6, where the timing belt has to come off). Shops often suggest replacing the crankshaft sensor at the same visit; that is a separate job.
held_reason: No labor time printed with a unit for the economy or luxury class, and the luxury class has only one parts source; the midsize and truck classes each rest on a single stated time from the same bulletin.
